## Ancient Greece on a timeline

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.timeline}
- **776 BC** · The first recorded {{< vocab "Olympic Games" >}} at Olympia.
- **About 508 BC** · Athens starts a {{< vocab "democracy" >}}.
- **447–432 BC** · The Parthenon {{< vocab "temple" >}} is built in Athens.
- **399 BC** · The {{< vocab "philosopher" >}} Socrates dies in Athens.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
![](images/parthenon-west.jpg){.photo fig-alt="The Parthenon, a ruined marble temple with rows of columns, under a blue sky"}

[The Parthenon in Athens today, about 2,450 years old.]{.photo-caption}
:::
::::

::: {.small-note}
BC means "before Christ": the years count *down* toward year 1. So 776 BC came before 508 BC.
:::

::: notes
Ask: which of these words do you already know in Chinese? We'll meet each one this unit.
:::

## Mountains and sea

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Greece is a rocky {{< vocab "peninsula" >}} with many islands.
- Mountains split the land into small valleys.
- Each valley grew its own {{< vocab "city-state" >}}: one city and its farms.
- The sea connected them. Greeks traded by ship and started a {{< vocab "colony" >}} wherever they found good land.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(card_grid(pick(terms, "peninsula", "colony"), zh=True))
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Ask: why would mountains make it hard for one king to rule all of Greece? (Hard to travel, hard to send armies, people stayed in their own valley.)
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis

```

## Athens and Sparta

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note title="Athens 雅典" icon=false}
- A {{< vocab "democracy" >}}: {{< vocab "citizen" text="citizens" >}} voted on laws
- Famous for plays, art and {{< vocab "philosopher" text="philosophers" >}}
- A strong navy and lots of trade
- Boys went to school to read, write and speak in public
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-warning title="Sparta 斯巴达" icon=false}
- Two kings and a council of elders
- Life was built around the army
- Boys left home at 7 to train as soldiers
- The strongest army on land in Greece
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Both were city-states, only a few days' walk apart, but life was very different. They fought each other in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC), which Sparta won.
:::

## How democracy worked in Athens

- The {{< vocab "assembly" >}} met about 40 times a year on a hill called the Pnyx.
- Any {{< vocab "citizen" >}} could stand up and speak.
- Then they voted, usually by raising their hands: {{< vocab "vote" >}}.
- In court, juries of hundreds of citizens voted with small tokens.

::: {.small-note}
*Demos* = people, *kratos* = power. Democracy = power of the people.
:::

## Who could vote?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Could vote" icon=false}
Free adult men with Athenian parents
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-warning title="Could not vote" icon=false}
- Women
- Enslaved people
- Foreigners living in Athens
:::
:::
::::

Only a small part of the people living in Athens were {{< vocab "citizen" text="citizens" >}}.

::: notes
Discussion: Was Athens a real democracy? Who would you add to the voters? How is this different from democracies today?
:::
